reverse_outline.summary: A sale lost between storefront and warehouse illustrates handoff failures; the guide names sixteen patterns to recognize and remedy them
Patterns grow from reasonable local decisions and travel in chains from an unowned origin; fix ownership, not blame
How each entry is structured, which examples are fictional versus public, and what follows the catalog
The four families are presented in the order a newcomer meets them: truth, integration, platform and change, governance
A warning sign only prompts investigation; confirm it by asking for the supporting number
Opening quote for Phantom Stock: site showed stock the warehouse no longer had
Phantom Stock symptom: storefront stock is a stale copy and pickup promises already-sold items
Phantom Stock cause: channels sell from delayed copies that several tools can change
Phantom Stock cost: cancellations and penalties, with research showing most inventory records are inaccurate
Kestrel & Pine's layered stock syncs let a sold-out jacket oversell 1,340 units at about EUR 96,000 cost
The store-pickup pilot repeated the problem through nightly stock updates
Even a vendor's own stock figure lags by seconds, per commercetools documentation
Phantom Stock remedy: one stock writer, events, central available-to-promise, reconciled copies (Waypoint W1)
Book chapters covering inventory, fact ownership and drift measurement for Phantom Stock
Opening quote for Schrödinger's Order: three systems report three different statuses
Schrödinger's Order symptom: conflicting statuses, missing messages, split shipments without status
Cause: money, shipments and returns have separate states but no record keeps them apart
Cost: order-status questions dominate support contacts, plus lost invoices and duplicate shipments
A split Kestrel & Pine order showed Delivered, In picking and Not invoiced for six days, generating 11 tickets
Shopify itself keeps several status families on one order
Remedy: one order record with separate money, shipment and return states and a computed summary (W2)
Book chapters on order management, service view and ERP integration for this pattern
Opening quote for Familiar Stranger: uncertain whether online and store customers are the same person
Familiar Stranger symptom: stores can't see online orders; data requests span many systems
Cause: each channel keeps its own customer table and nobody owns matching them
Cost: duplicate marketing, blind service, wrong loyalty counts and inability to meet GDPR deadlines
Eva exists as four unlinked records at Kestrel & Pine, so online loyalty waits for a unified customer record
Shopify deprecating legacy customer accounts shows identity must be rebuilt
Remedy: a customer master with one identifier, matching rules, linked channel records, privacy served from it
Book chapters on identity, privacy requests and why loyalty depends on them
Opening quote for Boomerang: a return refunded twice
Boomerang symptom: two refund issuers, stock rising at scan, spreadsheet credit notes
Cause: returns span goods, money and books with three owners and no defined refund trigger
Cost: high return and fraud rates; payment providers warn about double refunds
Kestrel & Pine refunded 212 returns twice, sending EUR 19,400 out twice
Unallocated stacked discounts caused 190 jacket refunds above the price paid
Shopify separates return money from reverse fulfillment and defines dispositions
Remedy: one return record, warehouse disposition as sole trigger, single refunding system, daily match
Book chapters on returns, payments and credit notes
Opening quote for Price Nobody Can Explain: different prices across channels
Symptom: prices in five systems, uncontrolled discount stacking, refunds at unpaid prices
Cause: many price setters, per-system copies, silent import failures, lingering promotion settings
Cost: margin, parity penalties and EU Omnibus prior-price compliance exposure
A failed agency import left German prices wrong for nine days, losing margin and drawing a parity warning
An unreverted combination setting stacked discounts on 2,860 Black Friday orders, costing about EUR 52,000
No public incident cited; the rules themselves require a 30-day price history per SKU and channel
Remedy: price ownership, dated price events, price history, ordered promotions, reconciliation, frozen order prices
Book chapters on pricing, promotions and channel parity
Opening quote for Spaghetti Junction: many integrations, many unowned, several writing stock
Symptom: many tools move the same fact on different paths and nobody has a list
Cause: each point-to-point connector was the quickest local fix
Cost: undiagnosable incidents and upgrades; surveys show integration complexity is a major concern
Kestrel & Pine's inventory found 34 integrations, 13 unowned, few reconciled, six stock writers
Zalando replaced 100+ disconnected interfaces with a single developer portal
Remedy: owned, contracted integration inventory, events through one place, reconciliation per copy (W5)
Book chapters on integration styles, ERP flows and ownership
Opening quote for Message in a Bottle: sender disclaims responsibility for delivery
Symptom: retries duplicate orders or refunds, dropped messages strand paid orders
Cause: delivery is at-least-once with vendor retry limits, yet integrations assume exactly-once
Cost: duplicates, losses, drift and peak backlogs, as Zalando's event pipeline showed
Throttled WMS order creation delayed 8,000 Black Friday orders past their delivery promise
Stripe warns fulfillment can't rely on customers reaching the landing page
Remedy: idempotency keys, handled-event records, fetch from owner, dead-letter queues, reconciliation
Book chapters on idempotency and reconciliation, integration style and payments
Opening quote for Pulled Rug: a vendor notice went to someone who had left
Symptom: calls to retired versions, chargebacks, unread changelogs
Cause: vendors announce changes but the merchant has no dependency record, reader or test
Cost: stale stock, strikes and rewrites; Amazon and bol API sunsets show public calendars
A retired API version silently broke bol stock updates for two days after a misdirected notice
A wholesale partner deducted EUR 14,200 for despatch advices mismatching delivered goods
Shopify changed stock-state meaning and runs a versioning calendar merchants must track
Remedy: pinned versions, sunset dates, role mailbox, partner cards, contract tests, packed-goods despatch advices
Book chapters on API versioning and EDI partners
Opening quote for First Snowfall: stable all year until peak day
Symptom: storefront survives peak while syncs and queues fail
Cause: designs and load tests target ordinary hours and the storefront, not the integrations
Cost: oversells and missed promises on peak day, as Target's 2011 crashes showed
Kestrel & Pine's Black Friday platform held but its stock sync and WMS queue broke
Lacking a kill switch, a card-testing bot attack led the payment provider to pause the account
Shopify load-tests its platform heavily, but merchants must size their own connectors
Remedy: test integrations at peak multiples, degrade switches, change freeze, runbook
Book chapters on peak planning, the peak-day journey and order queue sizing
Opening quote for Giant's Boots: copying big companies' architectures
Symptom: small teams adopting composable or headless architectures sized for giants
Cause: giants publish good work and vendors sell heavy shapes, skipping the question of need
Cost: expense and slower change; Segment and Prime Video reversals show it
Kestrel & Pine declined composable and headless rebuild pitches and chose to stay on the platform (W4)
Zalando narrowing its event-driven approach shows giants revising choices others copied
Remedy: measure scale factors and add capabilities only for measured problems
Book chapters on architecture styles, stay-and-surround, and stage tests
Opening quote for Burned Bridge: go-live and old platform shutdown on the same day
Symptom: big-bang migrations with old system switched off, dated just before peak
Cause: big bang looks cheaper and each risk seemed fine in demos
Cost: lost sales, recoverable only when old platform kept, as Finish Line showed
Kestrel & Pine plans a seam-by-seam OMS and PIM rollout through 2027
Target's pre-holiday 2011 launch shows a date chosen against the calendar
Remedy: migrate by seams, keep old path through a peak, parallel runs, rollback rehearsal, exit design
Book chapters on migration, strangler pattern and replatforming cases
Opening quote for Forked Platform: customizations block upgrades
Symptom: modified vendor files, checkout scripts, unused apps
Cause: customizations were fastest and nobody owns upgradeability
Cost: lost features, security exposure and forced migrations on vendor deadlines (Adobe, Shopify)
Kestrel & Pine's customized theme but untouched checkout makes staying on the platform possible
41 apps, several unused or writing inventory, now governed by an owner rule removing stock-writing rights
No public merchant cost cited; vendor sunsets only show when forks break
Remedy: owned upgradeability, supported extension points, customization register, routine upgrades
Book chapters on extensibility, storefront and checkout
Opening quote for One Size Fits None: merging brands onto a group platform for synergies
Symptom: one tenant forcing negotiation across differing brands, or unmeasured duplication
Cause: sharing is decided on cost while operational differences stay invisible
Cost: sharing slows change and spreads peaks; separation duplicates contracts and integrations
Kestrel & Pine's three storefronts share one tenant appropriately because they share everything relevant
Defined triggers would prompt review; group-sharing decision deferred to 2029
Zalando and ABOUT YOU sharing logistics and payments is a public sharing decision
Remedy: decide sharing per capability, sharing only scale-economy same-rule capabilities, quantify benefit first
Book chapters on tenancy, group-stage signals and Zalando's sharing
Opening quote for Lynchpin: only one absent consultant understands the mappings
Symptom: undocumented connectors and knowledge in one head
Cause: specialists are efficient and exit plans show no return until needed
Cost: outages tied to absences and programs ending on vendor dates (Shopify logistics, Zalando Connected Retail)
Kestrel & Pine's EDI, ERP connector and five unowned integrations depended on single people
Connected Retail is a channel retired by its platform owner
Remedy: ownership map, merchant-held contracts, second person per mapping, exit cost at purchase
Book chapters on ownership, exit pricing and partner knowledge
Opening quote for Long Fuse: a regulatory deadline discovered late
Symptom: mandates learned by chance and no accessibility audit
Cause: rules arrive per topic and country, unread and unowned
Cost: fines and blocked invoices; Belgian e-invoicing, accessibility, PCI and German dates are public
Kestrel & Pine met the Belgian e-invoicing mandate via Peppol
A 2027 regulatory calendar assigns owners and dates to remaining rules
Belgium gave fifteen months' notice before fines
Remedy: owned regulatory calendar and vendor conformance in procurement
Book chapters on regulation, e-invoicing and PCI security
Opening quote for Secret Agent: an unknown actor changed 600 stock levels
Symptom: scripts and apps share an admin key and write beside official feeds
Cause: apps are easy to add and broadly permitted; AI agents enter the same way with more autonomy
Cost: phantom stock, price drift, compromised checkout as in polyfill.io
A pre-order app and the price script wrote data unseen at Kestrel & Pine
Waypoint responds with integration ownership (W5) and agent readiness without agents (W8)
Polyfill.io shows checkout code changing hands unnoticed
Remedy: owned actors with own credentials, least privilege, approval thresholds, human gate for AI agents
Book chapters on app governance, security and agentic commerce
Four scale stages; most patterns originate at Growing and cost most at Omnichannel
Kestrel & Pine traces eight of ten incidents to Growing-stage designs

reverse_outline.summary: Patterns set each other up in three cross-family chains, and repairs hold at chain origins

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How the Patterns Reinforce Each Other ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Integration chain: unowned connectors lead to lost messages and then truth patterns, exposed at peak

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How the Patterns Reinforce Each Other ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Governance chain: unwatched dependencies enable Pulled Rug, Secret Agent and Long Fuse

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How the Patterns Reinforce Each Other ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Platform chain: copied decisions lead to forks, burned bridges and ill-fit group sharing

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How the Patterns Reinforce Each Other ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: Familiar Stranger runs under all chains because nobody owns customer matching

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How the Patterns Reinforce Each Other ¶6
reverse_outline.summary: Waypoint sequences fixes from origins: ownership first, then hubs, trustworthy copies, keep platform
Promises break away from where they were made, so remedies are ownership, contracts and reconciliation, not new platforms
The opening lost sale is a Message in a Bottle; ask who owns the origin before incidents, in three situations
In design reviews, walk an order through handoffs checking for patterns
In vendor demos, ask to see pattern scenarios rather than features
In due diligence, request ownership documents; each missing one signals an unowned pattern
Hand-off to the next page introducing Kestrel & Pine
